name: Réti Opening
summary: The Réti Opening (1.Nf3 d5 2.c4) is a hypermodern flank system that fianchettoes and pressures d5 from the wing.
intro: The Réti Opening arises after 1.Nf3 d5 2.c4, a hypermodern flank strategy in which White declines to occupy the centre with pawns and instead undermines Black's d5-pawn from the wing. Combined with a kingside fianchetto of g3 and Bg2, it aims to control the central squares from a distance and frequently transposes into English, Catalan, or Queen's Gambit structures.

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The Réti embodies the hypermodern idea of controlling the centre with pieces rather than occupying it with pawns. The thrust 2.c4 challenges Black's d5-pawn from the flank: if Black defends with ...c6 or ...e6, White fianchettoes and keeps up the pressure, and if Black grabs the pawn with ...dxc4, White regains it comfortably while developing smoothly. The flexible, non-committal move order lets White postpone central decisions until Black has shown his hand.

A hallmark of the system is its transpositional richness. Depending on how Black responds, the Réti can flow into an English, a Catalan, or a King's Indian Attack, so White uses it as a move-order weapon to steer toward structures he knows well. The double fianchetto, adding b3 and Bb2 to the kingside setup, is a characteristic device that trains both bishops on the central squares from either wing.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: Black has three principal replies to 2.c4. The space-grabbing 2...d4 pushes the pawn forward, when White undermines it with e3 and often b4; the solid 2...e6 or 2...c6 shores up d5 and can lead to Slav- or Catalan-like positions; and the acquisitive 2...dxc4 accepts the pawn, after which White regains it with moves such as Na3 or e3 and a timely Qa4.

White's development can take several shapes: the classical Réti fianchetto, the King's Indian Attack with g3, Bg2, O-O, d3, Nbd2 and a later e4, or a direct transposition into the Catalan or English. For his part, Black often develops the light-squared bishop actively with ...Bf5 or ...Bg4 before playing ...e6, avoiding the passive piece that can arise in closed queen's-pawn structures.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The opening is named after Richard Réti, a leading figure of the hypermodern school of the 1920s who, alongside players such as Nimzowitsch and Tartakower, argued that the centre could be dominated from afar. Réti famously used flank development to defeat the reigning World Champion José Raúl Capablanca at New York 1924, a landmark result that helped popularise these ideas. The opening has remained a respected, flexible choice for players who prefer manoeuvring and structural nuance to early central confrontation.

keyIdeas: 1.Nf3 delays central pawns, keeping a flexible hypermodern setup.
2.c4 attacks d5 from the flank instead of contesting it with e4 or d4.
A kingside fianchetto (g3, Bg2) presses along the long light diagonal.
The opening is highly transpositional, flowing into English or Catalan lines.
A double fianchetto (b3/Bb2 and g3/Bg2) targets the centre from both wings.
Against ...dxc4 White regains the pawn comfortably and develops freely.

white: Fianchetto with g3 and Bg2 to pressure d5 and the long diagonal.
Keep move-order flexibility and transpose to a favourable structure.
Undermine an advanced ...d4 pawn with e3 and b4 or c3.
Add a second fianchetto with b3 and Bb2 for extra central control.
Regain the pawn smoothly if Black snatches on c4.
black: Support d5 with ...c6 or ...e6 for a solid, Slav-like structure.
Develop the light-squared bishop actively with ...Bf5 or ...Bg4.
Grab space with ...d4, gaining central territory.
Accept with ...dxc4 and aim for quick, harmonious development.
Play for ...e5 to seize the centre if White stays passive.
